content_html:
VioLens is an open source tool for inspecting HTTP and HTTPS traffic, built as a successor to Fiddler Web Debugger (Fiddler Classic). Progress Software changed Fiddler Classic's license in 2026 to allow only non-commercial use. VioLens is free for any use, under the MIT license. It's an independent project, not affiliated with Progress or Telerik (see Relationship to Fiddler).

VioLens was called CLeARINET until version 0.2. It isn't Eric Lawrence's Clearinet, a separate project (see Clearinet). Settings, rules and extensions from a CLeARINET install carry over the first time VioLens runs (see the User Guide's "Upgrading from CLeARINET").

Downloads, the User Guide and more are at violens.dev. Questions and ideas are welcome on Discord; bugs go in issues.

Status

1.0 release candidate. The features planned for 1.0 are in, and the proxy engine's public API is frozen. What's left before 1.0 itself is hands-on testing on macOS and on KDE Plasma (see Known limitations). Feedback and issues are welcome.

What it does

Capturing

  • Captures http:// and HTTPS traffic through a local proxy. HTTPS is decrypted with a root certificate made for your install and trusted for your account, as Fiddler Classic does it. Tools > Remove Root Certificate (and the Windows uninstaller) takes it away again. Hosts that pin their certificates can be left encrypted (Tools > Connections).
  • Runs on Windows, macOS and Linux (x86-64, as an AppImage or a .tar.gz).
  • Becomes the system proxy while it runs: WinINET on Windows, networksetup on macOS, and GNOME's or KDE Plasma's settings on Linux. If a previous run crashed or was killed, the next one puts your proxy settings back.
  • HTTP/2, on by default: browsers use it with VioLens for HTTPS sites, and VioLens uses it with sites that offer it, falling back to HTTP/1.1. A Version column shows what each side used, and gRPC's trailers come through.
  • WebSocket messages, live, in their own tab, with compressed and fragmented messages put back together.
  • Forwards through your network's proxy, including PAC scripts and automatic detection (WPAD), and signs in to it as you (Negotiate or NTLM) or with a user name and password.
  • Phones and other computers can use it as their proxy (Allow remote computers to connect), with a page at http://violens/ for installing the certificate on them.

Looking at what was captured

  • A session list with live filtering by text, method:, host: and status:, and Edit > Find Sessions (Ctrl+F) for searching bodies. Right-click a column header to find in that column, highlight repeated values, or choose and arrange columns.
  • Timing like browsers' developer tools: a waterfall column, a Timing tab, and a Statistics tab with totals, the slowest requests and easy wins.
  • Inspector tabs: Headers, Raw, JSON, Tree (JSON, CBOR or MessagePack as a tree), Markdown, WebView (an HTML page's text, and a script-free preview in your browser), WebForms, ImageView (with zoom, and a breakdown of any image bloat), Hex, Cookies (with sizes, and warnings for cookies browsers will refuse) and Notes.
  • Decompresses gzip, deflate, Brotli and zstd, alone or chained.
  • Compare Sessions (Ctrl+W) shows two sessions side by side, with each difference highlighted.
  • TextWizard (Ctrl+E) encodes and decodes Base64, URLs, HTML, hex and JavaScript escapes, and decodes JWTs, Unix times and SAML.

Changing traffic

  • Breakpoints on requests, responses, or narrower conditions (URL, method, status code): edit the paused message, then resume or abort it.
  • AutoResponder rules that answer matching requests without reaching the server: a file, a redirect, a delay, a dropped connection and more.
  • The Composer, for writing or editing a request and sending it, and Replay (R) for sending a captured one again.

Automating it

  • QuickExec (Alt+Q), Fiddler's command box, with suggestions as you type. violens-exec sends the same commands from scripts, like Fiddler's ExecAction.exe.
  • FiddlerScript: a CustomRules.js script can hook requests and responses, and add Rules-menu options, buttons, context-menu actions and columns. See the FiddlerScript Compatibility Design.
  • Extensions: a compiled .dll in the Extensions folder can add hooks, inspectors, and importers and exporters. Fiddler Classic extensions can be ported from source with few changes (Violens.CompatShim); the NetLog importer, the CSP Rule Collector and the Privacy Scanner are ported, and the installers include them as optional extensions. An optional legacy extension host on Windows runs extensions that need parts of WinForms .NET no longer has.

Files and settings

  • Saves and opens SAZ files, saves and imports HAR, and imports the plain HTTP in packet captures (.pcap, .pcapng).
  • Remembers its settings in a preferences.json that's the same on every platform. Administrators can lock settings or set defaults for everyone on a machine: with Group Policy or Intune on Windows, using the ADMX template each release includes, or with a policy.json file.
  • VioLens Capture, a separate one-window app like Fiddler's FiddlerCap: someone who isn't technical clicks Start, shows the problem, clicks Stop and saves a .saz for you. On Windows it's a single .exe that runs without installing.

Help > Documentation opens the User Guide, which covers all of this.

Getting started

You need the .NET 10 SDK.

dotnet restore VioLens.sln
dotnet build VioLens.sln
dotnet test VioLens.sln
dotnet run --project apps/Violens.DesktopUi

dotnet run --project apps/Violens.Capture runs VioLens Capture.

The first time you click Start, VioLens asks to trust a new root certificate, named DO_NOT_TRUST_ViolensRoot... after Fiddler Classic's convention. That's what lets it read HTTPS traffic on this computer.

  • Windows shows its own prompt.
  • macOS has no prompt for this, so VioLens asks first, then adds the certificate to your login keychain. Firefox doesn't read the keychain by default, so VioLens turns on its setting that does in each profile; restart Firefox if it was open.
  • Linux: VioLens asks first, then adds it to your browsers' certificate databases with certutil (from libnss3-tools or nss-tools, which you may need to install).

Nothing you capture leaves your computer unless you send it somewhere.

Documentation

  • Using the app: the User Guide, also under Help > Documentation in the app.
  • Building your own tool on the proxy engine: Embedding ProxyCore. The engine is on NuGet as Violens.ProxyCore, with the same version as each VioLens release.
  • Contributing, or curious how something works: the rest of docs/ has the design behind each part of the app, what was left out and why, and what's still to do.

Project layout

  • docs/: the User Guide, and the design docs (the project plan, the certificate, preferences, FiddlerScript and .NET extension designs, the Fiddler feature inventory and breakpoint research notes).
  • src/Violens.ProxyCore: the proxy engine, also on NuGet. The listener, HTTP parsing, sessions, breakpoints, AutoResponder, certificates, SAZ, HAR and packet capture files, the system proxy on each platform, and the preferences store. Only what other apps need is public; VioLens's own assemblies are listed in its AssemblyInfo.cs.
  • src/Violens.ProxyHost and src/Violens.ProxyHost.Client: the engine for apps on .NET Framework, as a small .NET 10 host program and a .NET Standard 2.0 library that talks to it over a named pipe. See the Embedding guide's "Apps on .NET Framework".
  • src/Violens.AppCore: VioLens's own logic outside the engine, such as Compare, TextWizard, QuickExec, the column layout, machine policy and VioLens Capture's CaptureSession.
  • src/Violens.Automation: the pipe violens-exec uses.
  • src/Violens.Extensibility: the inspector contract and the built-in inspectors, with their JSON tree, CBOR, MessagePack and Markdown readers.
  • src/Violens.Compatibility: FiddlerScript (FiddlerScriptRunner), compiled extensions (ExtensionHost), and Violens.CompatShim for extensions ported from source. The two compatibility design docs describe what's built and what isn't.
  • apps/Violens.DesktopUi: the Avalonia desktop app.
  • apps/Violens.Capture: VioLens Capture.
  • samples/EmbeddingSample: the Embedding guide's code as a console app, built with everything else so the guide stays accurate.
  • tools/Violens.Exec: violens-exec, built with Native AOT and shipped beside the app.
  • tools/Violens.SampleExtension: a small compiled extension that tests ExtensionHost against a real .dll.
  • tools/Violens.LegacyExtensionHost: the optional legacy extension host, a net48 process kept out of VioLens.sln so it can't affect the main build. See its README.
  • tools/Violens.DevHost: a console host from early development.
  • tests/: tests for the projects above, and tests/ExtensionPorts, which fetches real Fiddler Classic extensions at pinned commits, ports them and tests them (not in VioLens.sln; see its README).

Known limitations

  • macOS has had less use than Windows.
    • Certificates are trusted with the security tool in your login keychain, and the system proxy is set with networksetup for each network service.
    • CI checks the macOS build's signature and that it launches, but its tests don't run security or networksetup for real.
    • A full hands-on test is still to come: trust and removal, whether networksetup needs admin rights, recovery after a crash, and the notarized install.
    • Release .dmg files are signed and notarized when the repository's signing secrets are set. Other builds (forks, test builds) aren't, and macOS asks you to allow them once, in System Settings > Privacy & Security > Open Anyway.
  • Linux has been tested by hand on Ubuntu (GNOME), not yet on KDE Plasma.
    • The certificate goes into the NSS databases Chrome and Chromium read (~/.pki/nssdb) and into each Firefox profile, including the snap and Flatpak ones, with certutil, which must be installed. Restart Firefox if it was open.
    • It doesn't go into the system store that curl and most command-line tools read, because that needs root access and differs between distributions. The User Guide's "Linux" section has the commands.
    • The system proxy is set in GNOME's and KDE Plasma's settings. On other desktops, and for programs that only read http_proxy, set it by hand.
    • The certificate's private key is a file in your home folder, which is where .NET keeps keys on Linux. See SECURITY.md.
    • CI tests the Linux build and checks that the packages launch, but doesn't run certutil, gsettings or kwriteconfig for real. On Wayland, VioLens runs through XWayland.
    • x86-64 only. There's no Snap or Flatpak, because their sandboxes would stop VioLens changing proxy settings and certificate databases.
  • HTTP/2 has been used for real only on Windows so far. WebSockets stay on HTTP/1.1 connections (browsers arrange that), and there's no HTTP/3: browsers don't send it through a proxy, so they use HTTP/2.
  • Upstream proxies must be HTTP proxies. SOCKS isn't supported (a PAC script's SOCKS entries are skipped), and proxy sign-in supports Negotiate, NTLM and Basic, not Digest. On macOS and Linux, automatic proxy detection looks in DNS (wpad.<your domain>), not DHCP.
  • Compiled Fiddler Classic extensions need rebuilding. The main app loads extensions built against its own interfaces, which match Fiddler's at source level, so an existing .dll can't be dropped in. The optional legacy extension host runs unmodified extension source, recompiled against its own compatibility assembly, against live traffic.
  • One client certificate (mutual TLS) at a time, sent to every server that asks or to the hosts you list. Fiddler Classic's ClientCertificate.cer file and https-Client-Certificate flag aren't supported.
  • No web page rendering in the app. Avalonia has no browser control, so the WebView tab shows a page's text and opens a locked-down copy in your browser.
  • VioLens Capture is packaged for Windows only. On macOS and Linux, run it from source.
  • No preferences editor (about:config), no headless mode, and no built-in NetLog import. NetLog files open through the ported NetLog importer, one of the optional extensions.
  • Bodies are kept in memory. Each is capped at 64 MB, and the Keep setting limits how many sessions are held, but nothing is spilled to disk.

SECURITY.md explains how the certificate, the listener and the proxy host are protected, and what isn't covered yet.

Relationship to Fiddler

VioLens is an independent open source project. It isn't affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by Progress Software Corporation or Telerik. Fiddler, Fiddler Classic, Fiddler Everywhere, FiddlerCore and Telerik are trademarks of Progress Software Corporation. VioLens uses those names only to say what it's compatible with, and never presents itself, or anything it ships, as Fiddler.

VioLens is built from public documentation, the behavior anyone can observe (such as how the real tool lays out .saz files), and its own design, never from decompiled or leaked Fiddler source, and it contains no Fiddler code. CONTRIBUTING.md has the clean-room policy every contribution follows. The optional extensions in the installers are separate works by their authors, under their own licenses (see THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt beside them).

VioLens is inspired by Eric Lawrence's public writing about Fiddler, including his post Fiddler in 2026, and by his public Clearinet repository. It isn't his project, and he hasn't contributed code to it. It does build on some of his published open source work, under its own licenses: the ported NetLog importer, the CSP Rule Collector fork, and packet capture import, ported from Clearinet (see THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md).

Clearinet

Eric Lawrence is building his own free successor to Fiddler Classic, Clearinet, also under the MIT license. It and VioLens are separate projects that set out differently:

  • Clearinet is by the person who created Fiddler. Its main app is for Windows, built with WinForms to look and work like the Fiddler people already know, and to make porting Fiddler extensions and scripts easy. A cross-platform engine, Clearinet Core, is planned.
  • VioLens runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, with an Avalonia interface that follows Fiddler's layout without copying its look. Its engine is already on NuGet as Violens.ProxyCore, and Fiddler extensions are ported from source through Violens.CompatShim.

VioLens started as CLeARINET because Eric's Fiddler in 2026 post read as a call to action, and this project set out to answer it. It chose Avalonia to run on every platform, while Eric chose to stay with WinForms so existing Windows workflows keep working. With the two heading in different directions, it was renamed VioLens in version 0.2. If you only need Windows and want the closest thing to Fiddler Classic, Clearinet is worth following too. Both are free for any use.

Thanks to:

  • EJ Suter-Powell and Jose Gonzales, for testing VioLens on macOS.
  • Eric Lawrence, who created Fiddler, for the inspiration and the groundwork: two decades of Fiddler itself, and his public writing about how it works and what he'd do differently, which shaped much of VioLens's design. (This doesn't mean he endorses VioLens; see Relationship to Fiddler.)

License

MIT. See LICENSE.

content_html_zh:
VioLens is an open source tool for inspecting HTTP and HTTPS traffic, built as a successor to Fiddler Web Debugger (Fiddler Classic). Progress Software changed Fiddler Classic's license in 2026 to allow only non-commercial use. VioLens is free for any use, under the MIT license. It's an independent project, not affiliated with Progress or Telerik (see Relationship to Fiddler).

VioLens was called CLeARINET until version 0.2. It isn't Eric Lawrence's Clearinet, a separate project (see Clearinet). Settings, rules and extensions from a CLeARINET install carry over the first time VioLens runs (see the User Guide's "Upgrading from CLeARINET").

Downloads, the User Guide and more are at violens.dev. Questions and ideas are welcome on Discord; bugs go in issues.

地位

1.0 release candidate. The features planned for 1.0 are in, and the proxy engine's public API is frozen. What's left before 1.0 itself is hands-on testing on macOS and on KDE Plasma (see Known limitations). Feedback and issues are welcome.

它的作用

Capturing

  • Captures http:// and HTTPS traffic through a local proxy. HTTPS is decrypted with a root certificate made for your install and trusted for your account, as Fiddler Classic does it. Tools > Remove Root Certificate (and the Windows uninstaller) takes it away again. Hosts that pin their certificates can be left encrypted (Tools > Connections).
  • Runs on Windows, macOS and Linux (x86-64, as an AppImage or a .tar.gz).
  • Becomes the system proxy while it runs: WinINET on Windows, networksetup on macOS, and GNOME's or KDE Plasma's settings on Linux. If a previous run crashed or was killed, the next one puts your proxy settings back.
  • HTTP/2, on by default: browsers use it with VioLens for HTTPS sites, and VioLens uses it with sites that offer it, falling back to HTTP/1.1. A Version column shows what each side used, and gRPC's trailers come through.
  • WebSocket messages, live, in their own tab, with compressed and fragmented messages put back together.
  • Forwards through your network's proxy, including PAC scripts and automatic detection (WPAD), and signs in to it as you (Negotiate or NTLM) or with a user name and password.
  • Phones and other computers can use it as their proxy (Allow remote computers to connect), with a page at http://violens/ for installing the certificate on them.

Looking at what was captured

  • A session list with live filtering by text, method:, host: and status:, and Edit > Find Sessions (Ctrl+F) for searching bodies. Right-click a column header to find in that column, highlight repeated values, or choose and arrange columns.
  • Timing like browsers' developer tools: a waterfall column, a Timing tab, and a Statistics tab with totals, the slowest requests and easy wins.
  • Inspector tabs: Headers, Raw, JSON, Tree (JSON, CBOR or MessagePack as a tree), Markdown, WebView (an HTML page's text, and a script-free preview in your browser), WebForms, ImageView (with zoom, and a breakdown of any image bloat), Hex, Cookies (with sizes, and warnings for cookies browsers will refuse) and Notes.
  • Decompresses gzip, deflate, Brotli and zstd, alone or chained.
  • Compare Sessions (Ctrl+W) shows two sessions side by side, with each difference highlighted.
  • TextWizard (Ctrl+E) encodes and decodes Base64, URLs, HTML, hex and JavaScript escapes, and decodes JWTs, Unix times and SAML.

Changing traffic

  • Breakpoints on requests, responses, or narrower conditions (URL, method, status code): edit the paused message, then resume or abort it.
  • AutoResponder rules that answer matching requests without reaching the server: a file, a redirect, a delay, a dropped connection and more.
  • The Composer, for writing or editing a request and sending it, and Replay (R) for sending a captured one again.

Automating it

  • QuickExec (Alt+Q), Fiddler's command box, with suggestions as you type. violens-exec sends the same commands from scripts, like Fiddler's ExecAction.exe.
  • FiddlerScript: a CustomRules.js script can hook requests and responses, and add Rules-menu options, buttons, context-menu actions and columns. See the FiddlerScript Compatibility Design.
  • Extensions: a compiled .dll in the Extensions folder can add hooks, inspectors, and importers and exporters. Fiddler Classic extensions can be ported from source with few changes (Violens.CompatShim); the NetLog importer, the CSP Rule Collector and the Privacy Scanner are ported, and the installers include them as optional extensions. An optional legacy extension host on Windows runs extensions that need parts of WinForms .NET no longer has.

Files and settings

  • Saves and opens SAZ files, saves and imports HAR, and imports the plain HTTP in packet captures (.pcap, .pcapng).
  • Remembers its settings in a preferences.json that's the same on every platform. Administrators can lock settings or set defaults for everyone on a machine: with Group Policy or Intune on Windows, using the ADMX template each release includes, or with a policy.json file.
  • VioLens Capture, a separate one-window app like Fiddler's FiddlerCap: someone who isn't technical clicks Start, shows the problem, clicks Stop and saves a .saz for you. On Windows it's a single .exe that runs without installing.

Help > Documentation opens the User Guide, which covers all of this.

入门

You need the .NET 10 SDK.

dotnet restore VioLens.sln
dotnet build VioLens.sln
dotnet test VioLens.sln
dotnet run --project apps/Violens.DesktopUi

dotnet run --project apps/Violens.Capture runs VioLens Capture.

The first time you click Start, VioLens asks to trust a new root certificate, named DO_NOT_TRUST_ViolensRoot... after Fiddler Classic's convention. That's what lets it read HTTPS traffic on this computer.

  • Windows shows its own prompt.
  • macOS has no prompt for this, so VioLens asks first, then adds the certificate to your login keychain. Firefox doesn't read the keychain by default, so VioLens turns on its setting that does in each profile; restart Firefox if it was open.
  • Linux: VioLens asks first, then adds it to your browsers' certificate databases with certutil (from libnss3-tools or nss-tools, which you may need to install).

Nothing you capture leaves your computer unless you send it somewhere.

文档

  • Using the app: the User Guide, also under Help > Documentation in the app.
  • Building your own tool on the proxy engine: Embedding ProxyCore. The engine is on NuGet as Violens.ProxyCore, with the same version as each VioLens release.
  • Contributing, or curious how something works: the rest of docs/ has the design behind each part of the app, what was left out and why, and what's still to do.

项目布局

  • docs/: the User Guide, and the design docs (the project plan, the certificate, preferences, FiddlerScript and .NET extension designs, the Fiddler feature inventory and breakpoint research notes).
  • src/Violens.ProxyCore: the proxy engine, also on NuGet. The listener, HTTP parsing, sessions, breakpoints, AutoResponder, certificates, SAZ, HAR and packet capture files, the system proxy on each platform, and the preferences store. Only what other apps need is public; VioLens's own assemblies are listed in its AssemblyInfo.cs.
  • src/Violens.ProxyHost and src/Violens.ProxyHost.Client: the engine for apps on .NET Framework, as a small .NET 10 host program and a .NET Standard 2.0 library that talks to it over a named pipe. See the Embedding guide's "Apps on .NET Framework".
  • src/Violens.AppCore: VioLens's own logic outside the engine, such as Compare, TextWizard, QuickExec, the column layout, machine policy and VioLens Capture's CaptureSession.
  • src/Violens.Automation: the pipe violens-exec uses.
  • src/Violens.Extensibility: the inspector contract and the built-in inspectors, with their JSON tree, CBOR, MessagePack and Markdown readers.
  • src/Violens.Compatibility: FiddlerScript (FiddlerScriptRunner), compiled extensions (ExtensionHost), and Violens.CompatShim for extensions ported from source. The two compatibility design docs describe what's built and what isn't.
  • apps/Violens.DesktopUi: the Avalonia desktop app.
  • apps/Violens.Capture: VioLens Capture.
  • samples/EmbeddingSample: the Embedding guide's code as a console app, built with everything else so the guide stays accurate.
  • tools/Violens.Exec: violens-exec, built with Native AOT and shipped beside the app.
  • tools/Violens.SampleExtension: a small compiled extension that tests ExtensionHost against a real .dll.
  • tools/Violens.LegacyExtensionHost: the optional legacy extension host, a net48 process kept out of VioLens.sln so it can't affect the main build. See its README.
  • tools/Violens.DevHost: a console host from early development.
  • tests/: tests for the projects above, and tests/ExtensionPorts, which fetches real Fiddler Classic extensions at pinned commits, ports them and tests them (not in VioLens.sln; see its README).

已知的限制

  • macOS has had less use than Windows. Certificates are trusted with the security tool in your login keychain, and the system proxy is set with networksetup for each network service. CI checks the macOS build's signature and that it launches, but its tests don't run security or networksetup for real. A full hands-on test is still to come: trust and removal, whether networksetup needs admin rights, recovery after a crash, and the notarized install. Release .dmg files are signed and notarized when the repository's signing secrets are set. Other builds (forks, test builds) aren't, and macOS asks you to allow them once, in System Settings > Privacy & Security > Open Anyway.
  • Linux has been tested by hand on Ubuntu (GNOME), not yet on KDE Plasma. The certificate goes into the NSS databases Chrome and Chromium read (~/.pki/nssdb) and into each Firefox profile, including the snap and Flatpak ones, with certutil, which must be installed. Restart Firefox if it was open. It doesn't go into the system store that curl and most command-line tools read, because that needs root access and differs between distributions. The User Guide's "Linux" section has the commands. The system proxy is set in GNOME's and KDE Plasma's settings. On other desktops, and for programs that only read http_proxy, set it by hand. The certificate's private key is a file in your home folder, which is where .NET keeps keys on Linux. 请参阅 SECURITY.md。 CI tests the Linux build and checks that the packages launch, but doesn't run certutil, gsettings or kwriteconfig for real. On Wayland, VioLens runs through XWayland. x86-64 only. There's no Snap or Flatpak, because their sandboxes would stop VioLens changing proxy settings and certificate databases.
  • HTTP/2 has been used for real only on Windows so far. WebSockets stay on HTTP/1.1 connections (browsers arrange that), and there's no HTTP/3: browsers don't send it through a proxy, so they use HTTP/2.
  • Upstream proxies must be HTTP proxies. SOCKS isn't supported (a PAC script's SOCKS entries are skipped), and proxy sign-in supports Negotiate, NTLM and Basic, not Digest. On macOS and Linux, automatic proxy detection looks in DNS (wpad.<your domain>), not DHCP.
  • Compiled Fiddler Classic extensions need rebuilding. The main app loads extensions built against its own interfaces, which match Fiddler's at source level, so an existing .dll can't be dropped in. The optional legacy extension host runs unmodified extension source, recompiled against its own compatibility assembly, against live traffic.
  • One client certificate (mutual TLS) at a time, sent to every server that asks or to the hosts you list. Fiddler Classic's ClientCertificate.cer file and https-Client-Certificate flag aren't supported.
  • No web page rendering in the app. Avalonia has no browser control, so the WebView tab shows a page's text and opens a locked-down copy in your browser.
  • VioLens Capture is packaged for Windows only. On macOS and Linux, run it from source.
  • No preferences editor (about:config), no headless mode, and no built-in NetLog import. NetLog files open through the ported NetLog importer, one of the optional extensions.
  • Bodies are kept in memory. Each is capped at 64 MB, and the Keep setting limits how many sessions are held, but nothing is spilled to disk.

SECURITY.md explains how the certificate, the listener and the proxy host are protected, and what isn't covered yet.

Relationship to Fiddler

VioLens is an independent open source project. It isn't affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by Progress Software Corporation or Telerik. Fiddler, Fiddler Classic, Fiddler Everywhere, FiddlerCore and Telerik are trademarks of Progress Software Corporation. VioLens is built from public documentation, the behavior anyone can observe (such as how the real tool lays out .saz files), and its own design, never from decompiled or leaked Fiddler source, and it contains no Fiddler code. CONTRIBUTING.md has the clean-room policy every contribution follows. VioLens is inspired by Eric Lawrence's public writing about Fiddler, including his post Fiddler in 2026, and by his public Clearinet repository. It isn't his project, and he hasn't contributed code to it. It does build on some of his published open source work, under its own licenses: the ported NetLog importer, the CSP Rule Collector fork, and packet capture import, ported from Clearinet (see THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md).

Clearinet

  • Clearinet is by the person who created Fiddler. Its main app is for Windows, built with WinForms to look and work like the Fiddler people already know, and to make porting Fiddler extensions and scripts easy. A cross-platform engine, Clearinet Core, is planned.
